title: JESUS DEFENDED THE WOMAN WHO STOPPED WORKING—AND HIS REASON WILL CONFRONT EVERYTHING YOU BELIEVE ABOUT SERVING GOD
paragraphs: JESUS DEFENDED THE WOMAN WHO STOPPED WORKING—AND HIS REASON WILL CONFRONT EVERYTHING YOU BELIEVE ABOUT SERVING GOD

Mary sat at His feet. Martha worked until she was overwhelmed. Both loved Jesus. But when Martha asked Him to correct her sister, His answer revealed a dangerous mistake even devoted Christians can make: becoming so busy doing things for Jesus that they stop listening to Jesus.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.

You wake up tired. You pray while thinking about everything you still need to accomplish. You serve at church, help your family, carry responsibilities nobody seems to notice, and somehow convince yourself that if you could just do a little more, perhaps God would finally be pleased.
You are not running away from Jesus.
You are running yourself into the ground trying to serve Him.
And sometimes, in the quiet moments when nobody is watching, a painful question rises from somewhere deep inside your heart.
"Lord, don't You see how hard I'm trying?"
That question is older than you think.
It once came from a woman who welcomed Jesus into her home, worked to make Him comfortable, and eventually became so overwhelmed that she questioned why He wasn't doing something about her sister.
Her name was Martha.
And what Jesus said to her has the power to expose one of the most heartbreaking misunderstandings in the Christian life.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to your intimacy with Christ is not an obvious sin pulling you away.
Sometimes it is a good thing consuming so much of your attention that you can no longer hear His voice.
And before you decide that Martha was simply wrong and Mary was simply right, you need to understand something.
Martha wasn't the enemy of this story.
She was a woman who loved Jesus.
And that is precisely what makes this encounter so painfully personal.
Luke 10:38–42 brings us into a home where two sisters respond differently to the same extraordinary Guest.
Jesus enters their village, and Martha welcomes Him into her house.
That detail matters.
Martha was not indifferent to Christ. She did not reject His presence. She opened her home to Him.
Hospitality in the ancient world was a serious responsibility. Welcoming guests meant providing care, food, and attention. It was an expression of generosity, not merely a social performance.
Martha's service was not inherently sinful.
In fact, the New Testament repeatedly commends hospitality and serving others.
But something began happening inside that home.
While Martha was occupied with the preparations, Mary sat at Jesus' feet, listening to His teaching.
Imagine the scene.
The responsibilities were multiplying. Food needed attention. Guests needed care. Work remained unfinished.
And there was Mary.
Sitting.
Listening.
Apparently doing nothing to relieve her sister's burden.
You can almost feel Martha's frustration building.
Perhaps she looked toward Mary once, expecting her to notice.
Perhaps she waited for her to get up.
Perhaps she wondered why Jesus Himself wasn't correcting the situation.
Luke does not tell us these imagined details, but it does tell us what eventually happened.
Martha approached Jesus and said:
"Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me."
—Luke 10:40, KJV
Read those words slowly.
"Lord, dost thou not care..."
There it is.
The wound beneath the workload.
Martha was not merely asking for assistance.
Her question challenged whether Jesus cared about what she was experiencing.
And if you have ever carried responsibilities while watching other people seem to live with fewer burdens, you may understand her more than you want to admit.
You keep showing up.
You keep giving.
You keep sacrificing.
Then one day, resentment begins creeping into places where gratitude used to live.
You start comparing your obedience with somebody else's.
You wonder why their life looks peaceful while yours feels unbearable.
You begin measuring your faithfulness by how much you suffer.
And somewhere along the way, your service becomes tangled with the desperate need to be noticed.
"Jesus, don't You see what I'm doing for You?"
But here comes the moment that changes everything.
Jesus did not humiliate Martha.
He did not tell her that serving was worthless.
He did not praise laziness or condemn responsibility.
Instead, He spoke her name twice.
"Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her."
—Luke 10:41–42, KJV
Martha.
Martha.
There is something deeply personal about that repetition.
In Scripture, repeated names can convey intense personal address. Here, the words of Jesus are corrective, but they are not cruel.
He sees her.
He understands that she is troubled.
And He addresses the deeper issue beneath her complaint.
The Greek text of Luke 10:41 reads:
Μάρθα Μάρθα, μεριμνᾷς καὶ θορυβάζῃ περὶ πολλά.
Martha, Martha, merimnas kai thorybazē peri polla.
A close translation is:
"Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things."
The verb μεριμνᾷς (merimnas) conveys being anxious or concerned.
The verb θορυβάζῃ (thorybazē) communicates being disturbed, agitated, or troubled.
Jesus was identifying the anxious turmoil that had overtaken Martha.
He was not declaring that preparing food was evil.
He was showing her that something had gone wrong in the way her responsibilities were governing her heart.
And Luke had already given us a clue.
In verse 40, the Greek word used to describe Martha's condition is περιεσπᾶτο (periespato), commonly translated as "distracted."
It carries the sense of being pulled away or diverted.
That is the tragedy.
Martha had welcomed Jesus into her home, yet the demands of hosting Him had drawn her attention away from the very One she welcomed.
She was serving the Guest while missing the opportunity to receive from Him.
And suddenly, this ancient story stops feeling ancient.
Because how many of us are doing the same thing?
We open our Bibles only to prepare a sermon, but rarely to sit humbly beneath the Word ourselves.
We sing worship songs while our minds are consumed by performance.
We work tirelessly in ministry, yet become impatient with the people we are supposed to love.
We build Christian projects, manage church responsibilities, organize outreach programs, and fill our schedules with religious activity.
But when was the last time we opened Scripture without rushing?
When was the last time we prayed without treating prayer like another task to finish?
When was the last time we confessed our sins without immediately trying to prove that we were still useful?
This is where Martha's story becomes uncomfortable.
Because it reveals that a person can be involved in genuinely good work while allowing anxiety, comparison, and resentment to distort the experience of serving Christ.
And the most frightening part?
We may not recognize what is happening until our exhaustion begins turning into accusation.
Martha said, "Lord, dost thou not care...?"
Notice how suffering had begun affecting her perception of Jesus.
The Lord who had come into her home was now being questioned about His compassion.
Have you ever done that?
Perhaps not aloud.
But in the private chambers of your heart?
"Lord, why am I the one carrying everything?"
"Why does nobody appreciate what I do?"
"Why do other Christians seem to have time for peace while I am constantly struggling?"
"Why do I feel so empty when I am doing so much for You?"
Those questions deserve to be brought honestly before God.
But they also deserve to be examined in the light of His Word.
Because there is a difference between serving Christ from love and trying to use service to secure the love Christ has already freely offered through His grace.
You cannot earn through exhaustion what Jesus gives through grace.
Ephesians 2:8–10 makes the order unmistakable.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works. Yet we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Did you catch that?
Good works matter.
But they are the fruit of God's saving grace, not the price we pay to obtain it.
We do not work our way into becoming worthy of Jesus.
We belong to Him through faith, and from that relationship flows a transformed life of obedience.
This is why the contrast between Mary and Martha is so important.
Mary was not presented as someone who despised work.
Luke simply tells us that she sat at the Lord's feet and listened to His teaching.
The Greek expression in Luke 10:39 includes:
παρακαθεσθεῖσα πρὸς τοὺς πόδας τοῦ κυρίου
parakathestheisa pros tous podas tou kyriou
Meaning, in context, that she sat at the Lord's feet.
That posture is significant.
In the biblical world, sitting at a teacher's feet could describe the position of someone receiving instruction. Acts 22:3 uses similar language when Paul speaks of being educated under Gamaliel.
Mary was not simply resting while Martha worked.
Mary was listening as a disciple.
And Jesus defended her opportunity to do so.
Think about the beauty of that moment.
In a society where domestic expectations often shaped women's daily responsibilities, Jesus affirmed Mary's decision to receive His teaching.
He did not tell her to abandon her place at His feet because her sister was overwhelmed.
He declared that she had chosen the good portion.
The Greek of Luke 10:42 includes:
Μαριὰμ γὰρ τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα ἐξελέξατο
Mariam gar tēn agathēn merida exelexato.
"For Mary has chosen the good portion."
The word μερίδα (merida) means a portion or share.
The language is especially striking in a home concerned with hospitality and preparations.
While Martha was troubled about many things, Mary had recognized the supreme importance of receiving the Lord's words.

Some manuscripts of Luke 10:42 preserve a longer reading referring to "few things" or "one," while others have the shorter expression "one thing is necessary." The textual variation affects the precise wording, but the central point remains clear: Jesus affirmed Mary's choice to listen to Him.
He was not establishing a universal rule that nobody should prepare meals.
He was teaching that even legitimate responsibilities must not displace what matters most.
And this is where many believers need to hear something they may have forgotten.
Jesus wants more than your productivity. He calls you into fellowship with Himself.
Not because obedience is optional.
Not because service is meaningless.
But because Christian service was never meant to replace communion with Christ.
John 15:5 records Jesus saying:
"I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing."
Notice the order again.
Abiding.
Then fruitfulness.
Remaining in Christ is not a reward reserved for Christians who have finished all their responsibilities.
It is the very source of spiritual life and fruitfulness.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to remember.
You have spent so long trying to prove that you are faithful.
You have been the dependable one.
The one who volunteers.
The one who stays late.
The one who keeps the family together.
The one who serves while quietly wondering whether anybody would notice if you finally stopped.
And beneath your dedication is a heart that has become weary.
You love Jesus.
But you are tired.
You believe in prayer.
But sometimes you are too overwhelmed to pray.
You know Scripture is precious.
But your Bible has become something you consult when you need an answer rather than a place where you patiently receive God's truth.
You are not necessarily living in open rebellion.
You may simply be living distracted.
And the story of Martha invites you to examine whether your responsibilities have become louder than the words of your Savior.
But please don't misunderstand the lesson.
Jesus was not asking Martha to become useless.
The same Lord who defended Mary also taught His disciples to love their neighbors through practical action.
Just before this account, Luke records the parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke 10:25–37.
There, love is demonstrated through costly compassion and practical care.
Then Luke shows us Mary listening at Jesus' feet.
These accounts belong together beautifully.
The Christian life is not a choice between loving service and attentive discipleship.
It requires both.
We listen to Christ, and we obey Him.
We receive His Word, and we put it into practice.
We love God, and that love expresses itself toward others.
The problem was not Martha's hands.
It was the turmoil that had overtaken her heart.
And Scripture gives us another reason not to reduce Martha to a cautionary tale.
In John 11, when her brother Lazarus died, Martha came to Jesus with grief and faith.
She confessed:
"Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world."
—John 11:27, KJV
What an extraordinary confession.
The same woman who once questioned whether Jesus cared also proclaimed Him to be the Christ, the Son of God.
Her earlier struggle did not define the entirety of her relationship with Him.
And that matters.
Because one difficult season does not have to become the final description of your faith.
You can be overwhelmed today and still grow in trust.
You can be corrected by Scripture without being rejected by Christ.
You can discover that your motives have become tangled and still respond with repentance.
You can admit that your service has become bitter and ask the Lord to renew your love.
Martha's story is not an invitation to shame exhausted Christians.
It is an invitation to return to the proper center of Christian life.
Jesus Christ Himself.
And there is an even deeper Gospel truth here.
Mary's place at Jesus' feet was not something she purchased with religious accomplishments.
She was receiving His teaching.
And every Christian who truly understands the Gospel must begin with this same posture of dependence.
Before we can offer anything acceptable to God, we must recognize what Christ has done for us.
We are sinners who cannot rescue ourselves through moral effort, religious activity, or ministry success.
Our deepest problem is not simply that we are busy.
It is that sin has separated us from the holy God who created us.
And no amount of church work can erase our guilt.
No number of sermons preached can purchase forgiveness.
No pile of good deeds can make the cross unnecessary.
But Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, came to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered by grace.
That is why the Gospel is such good news for the exhausted soul.
Your salvation does not rest on how much you accomplish for Jesus. It rests on what Jesus has accomplished for sinners.
This does not excuse spiritual laziness or disobedience.
Grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and live for Christ, as Titus 2:11–14 teaches.
But grace also destroys the illusion that we can earn our standing before God through relentless performance.
And perhaps that is the scandal hiding inside this beautiful encounter.
A woman was busy doing something honorable.
Another woman was quietly listening.
And Jesus defended the one who appeared to be accomplishing less.
Not because service had no value.
But because the Lord's presence and teaching were too precious to be treated as secondary.
From the outside, Mary might have looked unproductive.
From Jesus' perspective, she had chosen the good portion.
And now I want to ask you something.
Not as an accusation.
As an invitation to spiritual honesty.
If Jesus sat with you today, would you be able to stop long enough to listen?
Or would you immediately begin explaining everything you still needed to do?
Would you feel compelled to prove how useful you are?
Would you begin listing your sacrifices, your ministry responsibilities, your disappointments, your achievements?
Would you feel guilty for being still?
There is a place for hard work.
There is a place for sacrifice.
There is a place for serving others even when it costs us something.
But there must also be room in our lives for the Word of Christ to dwell richly within us.
For prayer.
For repentance.
For worship that is not performed for an audience.
For quiet obedience that nobody applauds.
For the kind of fellowship with God that reminds us why we began serving in the first place.
And sometimes the most faithful thing you can do is not add another religious activity to your schedule.
Sometimes it is to open your Bible, put away the distractions, and give your attention to what Jesus has said.
Not because you have earned a peaceful moment.
But because His Word is worthy of your attention.
If this story has exposed something in your heart, don't rush past it.
Maybe you have become resentful toward people who seem to be doing less than you.
Maybe your service has become an attempt to gain approval.
Maybe you have confused being indispensable to a ministry with being spiritually healthy.
Maybe you have been feeding everyone else while neglecting your own need for God's Word.
Maybe you have been so busy talking about Jesus that you have forgotten to listen to Him.
Bring that honestly before the Lord.
Confess what needs confessing.
Release the comparisons.
Ask Him to restore joy where resentment has grown.
And remember that repentance is not merely feeling bad about your spiritual condition.
It is turning back to God in faith and obedience.
Perhaps your prayer today is as simple as this:

"Lord Jesus, I have been distracted by so many things. Some are good. Some are necessary. But I have allowed them to occupy a place in my heart that belongs to You. Forgive my pride, my resentment, and my attempts to find worth in what I accomplish. Teach me to listen to Your Word. Give me wisdom to serve faithfully without making service my identity. Help me remember that You are my Savior, not my employer waiting for me to earn Your love. Restore my joy in You. Amen."
And if those words describe your struggle, I would love to hear from you.
You don't have to explain every detail publicly. A few honest words are enough.
Your experience may encourage someone who thinks their exhaustion means their faith has failed.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message more than you realize.
A mother who is overwhelmed.
A father quietly carrying financial and family burdens.
A pastor who has forgotten what it feels like to receive spiritual nourishment without preparing to give it away.
A ministry volunteer whose joy has slowly turned into resentment.
A believer who thinks God only values them when they are accomplishing something.
Because the goal is not to build a community impressed by religious activity.
It is to help people know, trust, love, and follow the Lord Jesus Christ.
That is also why Gospel Warrior continues creating and sharing Christian resources.
These resources are part of our commitment to making biblical nourishment accessible, especially to people who may not have the means to purchase books or other discipleship materials.
But continuing and expanding that work requires real resources.
And this is where I want to invite you into something meaningful.

Scripture teaches that supporting Gospel ministry is a worthy expression of generosity. Philippians 4:15–18 describes believers partnering with Paul through their gifts. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from a willing heart, not from compulsion.
It isn't.
Think of the person who might encounter the Gospel through a resource your generosity helped make possible.
The discouraged believer who discovers a devotional at exactly the right moment.
The young Christian who begins studying Scripture more seriously.
The person who has been drifting spiritually but finds a reason to open the Bible again.
We cannot promise what every reader will do with the resources they receive.
But we can continue working faithfully to make sound, Christ-centered teaching available.
And you can help make that possible.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation and opportunities to encourage faith in everyday life. They are not spiritual rewards, and purchasing them does not make anyone more favored by God.
We want to build a community where people are not simply consuming inspirational words but learning to follow Jesus faithfully.
Where the weary are encouraged.
Where the proud are called to repentance.
Where those struggling with sin are directed toward the mercy and holiness of Christ.
Where Scripture is not treated as decoration for motivational messages but as the authoritative Word of God.
And where every testimony of genuine transformation points away from human achievement and toward the Savior who makes redemption possible.
Because that is what this entire story has been about from the beginning.
Not which sister was more impressive.
Not whether cooking was less spiritual than listening.
Not whether Christians should abandon responsibility.
But whether Jesus Christ occupies His rightful place at the center of our lives.
Martha's work mattered.
Mary's listening mattered.
But Jesus mattered more than either woman's activity.
And the beautiful thing is that the Lord who corrected Martha was the same Lord she later confessed as the Christ, the Son of God.
His correction was not the end of her story.
And whatever the Lord is exposing in your heart today does not have to be the end of yours.
Maybe you have been serving with the wrong motives.
Maybe you have been living under the crushing pressure of trying to earn what only grace can give.
Maybe your relationship with God has become a long list of obligations, and you have forgotten the wonder of knowing Christ.
Return to His Word.
Return to prayer.
Return to the Gospel.
Not to escape the responsibilities He has entrusted to you, but to carry them with a heart increasingly shaped by His truth.
Let your service flow from faith rather than fear.
Let your generosity flow from love rather than guilt.
Let your obedience grow from gratitude rather than the desperate need to prove yourself.
And when you find yourself becoming anxious and troubled about many things, remember the gentle but searching words spoken inside that home long ago.
"Martha, Martha..."
Perhaps the most important thing Jesus was teaching her was not how to accomplish more.
It was how to recognize what must never be lost amid everything else.
The good portion.
His Word.
His presence.
His lordship.
His grace.
And as you leave this story, carry one final question into the ordinary pressures of your life:
Are you so busy making room for Jesus in your schedule that you have forgotten to give Him your attention?
Because the Savior who calls you to faithful service is also the Savior whose grace you desperately need.
You do not have to choose between loving Jesus and serving Him.
But you must never allow your service to become a substitute for loving, trusting, and listening to Him.
The most heartbreaking thing would be to spend your whole life working in the house for Jesus while continually neglecting the voice of the One who came to save you.
